blocks.text: Add new operations to a class hierarchy without changing its classes, by moving each operation into a separate visitor.

Each element has one `accept(visitor)` method that calls back the visitor method for its own type. That is **double dispatch**: the operation depends on both the visitor and the element's runtime class, which Java's single dispatch cannot do on its own.

items: **Stays stable:** the set of element types.
**Cost:** adding an element type forces every visitor to change.

blocks.text: Visitor makes new operations cheap and new element types expensive. Use it only when the hierarchy is stable and the operations keep growing.

walkthrough.note: One `visit` method per element type, generic in the result `R`. This interface is the complete list of element types the operations must handle.
Each `accept` calls the method for its own type, passing `this`. First dispatch picks `accept` by the element's class; the call inside picks the visitor's method.
An operation is one class. Recursion goes through `accept(this)`, never `instanceof`, so every node dispatches on its real type.
A second operation is added without touching `Expr`, `Num`, `Add` or `Mul`. Each visitor chooses its own result type.
The client builds one tree and runs two unrelated operations over it. A new element type would need a new `Visitor` method, breaking every visitor at compile time.

blocks.text: Static analysis passes over a compiler's syntax tree.

A compiler has maybe 40 stable node types, but its passes keep growing: name resolution, type checking, constant folding, lint rules, code generation, each maintained by a different team. Putting every pass inside the node classes makes the nodes unreadable. One visitor per pass keeps each algorithm in one file, and a new lint rule is a new class with no merge conflicts in the tree definition.
Payoff: each pass is a self-contained class, tested alone, and the node classes stay small.

lists.title: Use when
items: The element types are stable but operations keep being added.
An operation needs per-type logic across many unrelated classes.
You want an operation's code in one place instead of spread over the hierarchy.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: New element types appear often: every visitor must change.
The hierarchy is small; a sealed type with a `switch` is lighter.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: Visitors need access to element internals, which pressures encapsulation.
Recursion with `instanceof` instead of `accept` silently skips dispatch.
Traversal logic duplicated in every visitor; centralize it or use a base visitor.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A visitor for a hierarchy with two subtypes.
Visitors that only ever return `void` and mutate shared state.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Sealed types plus `switch` patterns add operations without `accept` boilerplate, with compiler-checked exhaustiveness.
Classic Visitor still fits when the library owns traversal or the hierarchy is not sealed.

rows.difference: Composite builds the tree; Visitor adds operations over it. The two are used together so often that a visitor usually owns the traversal.
An iterator hands you elements one by one of a uniform type. A visitor handles each concrete type differently and can return results while traversing.
Interpreter puts the operation inside each node, so adding an operation edits every class. Visitor externalizes it, trading that for the cost of adding node types.
Visitor is open for new operations and closed for new element types. It applies the open-closed principle along one axis only.

entries.name: ClassVisitor

entries.name: ParseTreeVisitor
entries.detail: The generated `<Grammar>Visitor<T>` extends it with one `visitX` method per labeled rule, and `accept` on each context node dispatches to it.

options.why: Each shape calls back the method for its own type, so an operation is chosen by both the op and the shape's class.
A strategy is a single interchangeable algorithm; here the interface has one method per element type.
Nothing changes which object handles later calls; the shapes are immutable data.
There are no children or recursive structure, only a double-dispatch hook.

exercises.scenario: A document model has 12 stable node types. Over the next year, different teams will add spell-check, HTML export, PDF export, accessibility audit and word count. Nobody expects new node types.

options.why: A stable hierarchy with a growing set of operations: each new operation is one class and no node changes.
Each operation would be a method added to all 12 node classes, owned by the model team.
It varies steps of one algorithm; these are unrelated operations over the same structure.
A strategy swaps one algorithm and cannot dispatch on the type of each node it meets.

exercises.explanation: The left child is inspected with `instanceof`, so a nested `Add` or `Mul` evaluates to 0. Recurse through `a.left().accept(this)` so every node dispatches on its real type.

template: interface Visitor<R> { R visitNum(Num n); R visitAdd(Add a); R visitMul(Mul m); }
record Num(int value) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visitNum(this); } }
record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visitAdd(this); } }
record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visitMul(this); } }

template: interface Visitor<R> { R visitNum(Num n); R visitAdd(Add a); R visitMul(Mul m); }
record Num(int value) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visitNum(this); } }
record Add(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visitAdd(this); } }
record Mul(Expr left, Expr right) implements Expr { public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visitMul(this); } }
public Integer visitNum(Num n) { return n.value(); }
public Integer visitAdd(Add a) { return a.left().accept(this) + a.right().accept(this); }
public Integer visitMul(Mul m) { return m.left().accept(this) * m.right().accept(this); } }

exercises.prompt: Explain Visitor in your own words: what is double dispatch, and what does the pattern cost?

modelAnswer.text: Visitor moves operations out of a hierarchy into visitor classes. Each element's accept calls the visit method for its own type, so the code that runs depends on both the visitor and the element class: double dispatch. New operations are cheap; new element types force every visitor to change.

keyPoints: accept calls back visitX(this) for the element's own type
Double dispatch: runtime types of both visitor and element decide
New operations are one new class; no element changes
New element types break every existing visitor
Sealed types and switch patterns are the modern alternative
